what: Herc Holdings rents construction and industrial equipment. It owns a fleet of excavators, loaders, aerial lifts, generators, pumps and specialty equipment and rents it by the day, week or month to contractors and industrial customers who would rather not own it.
customers: Construction contractors, industrial and energy companies, utilities, film and event producers, and government agencies needing equipment temporarily.
money: Rental revenue from a large fleet of construction and industrial equipment.
Sale of fleet retired from rental, plus delivery and service charges.
moat: Equipment rental is a scale and density business: the operator with the most branches near a job site can deliver faster and keep utilisation higher, which means better returns on the same machine. Buying fleet in volume also costs less per unit. Contractors increasingly rent rather than own, because owning ties up capital in machines that sit idle between jobs.
risks: Debt of $9.6B against $52.0M of cash is enormous relative to a $5.1B market value — the equity is a thin slice of the capital structure.
Reported net income of $123.0M gives a price/earnings ratio of 40.5, because interest and depreciation consume the profit.
Equipment rental is cyclical: when construction slows, utilisation and rental rates fall together.
Last year’s net margin was effectively zero, which shows how little cushion there is.
Twelve analysts average a $202.42 target against a $150.97 price, a 34% gap.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $1.1B against a $5.1B market value is a very high yield, at about 4.5 times free cash flow.
Revenue has grown strongly, from $2.1B in 2021 to $4.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $4.9B.
Branch density near job sites is a genuine advantage that improves utilisation on the same fleet.
Contractors are shifting from owning to renting, which grows the whole market independently of construction volumes.
The fleet is a real asset that can be sold into a strong used equipment market if needed.
watch: Fleet utilisation and rental rates. Those two numbers determine the return on the equipment, and both are disclosed.
view: Equipment rental is a better business than it sounds, for a reason worth spelling out. A contractor who owns an excavator has capital tied up in a machine that sits idle between jobs, pays to maintain it, and must sell it eventually. A contractor who rents pays only for the days used. That arithmetic has been pushing the industry from ownership to rental for twenty years, and it grows the rental market independently of how much construction is happening.

Within rental, the advantage is density. The operator with the most branches near a job site delivers faster, collects faster, and keeps each machine working more days a year — and utilisation is everything, because the cost of owning the machine is the same whether it is on a site or in a yard. Herc has built that network, and revenue from $2.1 billion to $4.9 billion reflects both the shift to renting and acquisitions.

The balance sheet is where this becomes a different kind of investment. Debt of $9.6 billion against $52 million of cash, on a $5.1 billion market value, means the equity is a thin residual on a much larger structure. The reported figures follow directly: $123 million of net income on $4.9 billion of revenue, a price/earnings ratio of 40.5, and a near-zero net margin last year, because interest and depreciation absorb the profit. The honest figure is $1.1 billion of free cash flow at about 4.5 times.

That leverage is standard for the industry — fleet is financeable collateral — and it cuts both ways sharply. In a construction upturn, utilisation and rates rise together and the equity return is enormous. In a downturn, both fall together while the debt stays fixed, and the equity absorbs it. Utilisation and rental rates are the two numbers, and they move at the same time, which is the uncomfortable part.
bull: The shift from owning to renting keeps growing the market while branch density lifts utilisation, and deleveraging on $1.1 billion of free cash flow transfers value to a thin equity.
bear: Construction slows, utilisation and rental rates fall together, and $9.6 billion of debt against a near-zero margin leaves the equity exposed.
